subsystems.name: Biosignal sensing array
subsystems.role: picks up tiny electrical signals from speech muscles (subvocalization) and, to a lesser extent, from the brain.
parts: dry EMG electrodes on the ear canal

subsystems.name: Analog front end
subsystems.role: amplifies and filters microvolt-level signals before digitization.

subsystems.name: On-board processor and AI decoder
subsystems.role: extracts features from the signals and translates them into text using a trained neural network.

subsystems.name: Wireless link and power
subsystems.role: sends decoded text to a phone or computer and keeps the earbud running.

subsystems.name: User feedback and fit
subsystems.role: confirms recognition and ensures the earbud stays comfortably in place.

buildSteps.title: Design the electrode interface
buildSteps.detail: Engineer dry electrodes that make stable contact with the ear canal skin without gel, and that are comfortable for hours.

buildSteps.title: Fabricate the flexible sensor array
buildSteps.detail: Print or laminate conductive traces and electrodes on a flexible polymer substrate that fits the ear canal shape.

buildSteps.title: Integrate the electronics
buildSteps.detail: Assemble the analog front end, processor, AI accelerator, Bluetooth radio and battery onto a miniature printed circuit board.

buildSteps.title: Collect training data
buildSteps.detail: Record EMG and EEG signals from many volunteers while they silently mouth words or sentences, paired with the intended text.

buildSteps.title: Train the decoding model
buildSteps.detail: Use machine learning to map signal features to phonemes or words, with per-user fine-tuning to handle individual anatomy.

buildSteps.title: Assemble the earbud
buildSteps.detail: Package the sensor array and electronics into a moisture-resistant shell, seal it, and attach the ear tip and charging contacts.

buildSteps.title: Calibrate and test
buildSteps.detail: Each user performs a short calibration; then accuracy, latency, comfort and safety are validated before use.

prerequisites.why: existing dry electrodes work for short-term ECG or EEG, but long-term, high-quality EMG in the ear is still a research challenge.
smartphone and earbud chips can run small AI models on a battery.
laboratory systems have recognised small sets of words from face and neck EMG, but not yet general speech.
ear-EEG can detect some brain states, but decoding imagined speech from it is not yet reliable.
small lithium-ion and emerging solid-state cells power earbuds for hours.

pathway.milestone: Laboratory prototypes recognise a few dozen subvocalized words using electrodes on the jaw or neck.
pathway.unlocks: Proof that muscle signals during silent speech can be decoded.

pathway.milestone: In-ear prototypes combine EMG and ear-EEG to decode short phrases in real time.
pathway.unlocks: Hands-free, silent messaging for users in noisy or quiet environments.

pathway.milestone: Commercial earbuds with a limited vocabulary for specific tasks (e.g., controlling a phone).
pathway.unlocks: First consumer products, though not yet general thought-to-text.

pathway.milestone: General-purpose thought-to-text with large vocabulary and minimal calibration.
pathway.unlocks: Seamless silent communication for anyone, including people with speech impairments.
